vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: screen-monitor
Version: 1.0.1

The skill is designed for screen sharing and analysis by an AI agent. It uses a local Node.js server (`references/backend-endpoint.js`) on port 18795 to receive screen frames via WebRTC from `web/screen-share.html`, saving them to `/tmp/clawdbot-screen-latest.png`. The `references/screen-analyze.sh` script then instructs the local `clawdbot agent` to analyze this image. While the WebRTC portal is accessible via LAN IP (`references/get-share-url.sh`) and declared as 'remote_access' in `manifest.json`, the user must explicitly initiate screen sharing, and all captured data is processed locally by the agent, not exfiltrated to external unauthorized endpoints. There is no evidence of malicious intent, unauthorized execution, or prompt injection attempts to subvert the agent's core directives.

llm.summary: This screen-sharing skill is purpose-aligned, but it exposes and stores sensitive screen frames with weak access controls and incomplete disclosure.

dimensions.detail: The backend uses port 18795, returns a LAN share URL, binds without an explicit loopback-only host, allows wildcard CORS, and accepts unauthenticated frame uploads, which is overbroad for sensitive screen content.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The manifest declares system dependencies and an optional ImageMagick install for screenshot fallback; no hidden installer, remote payload execution, or persistence installer was found.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill instructs agents to run local shell scripts and use browser control actions, but it does not clearly scope those capabilities or require a separate confirmation before capture, analysis, clicking, or typing.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: Captured screen frames and metadata are written to predictable /tmp paths with no evident cleanup on stop, no per-session isolation, and no restrictive file handling.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: Screen sharing, vision analysis, and browser interaction fit the stated purpose, but the implementation continuously uploads full-screen frames every 3 seconds and can fall back to OS-level screenshots, which is more sensitive than the short description makes clear.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review before installing. Only use this on trusted networks and with non-sensitive screens unless the skill is changed to bind locally or require authentication, limit uploads, clearly disclose capture cadence and retention, remove or confirm OS screenshot fallback, and clean up protected per-session frame files.
llm.findings:
[TP4] unexpected: The core screen-analysis purpose is coherent, but local network exposure and frame persistence are only partially disclosed; the concern is supported as under-disclosure rather than tool poisoning by itself.
[SQP-2] expected: Browser screen capture is expected for this skill, but the artifact confirms automatic repeated uploads to the backend every 3 seconds without a clear user-facing explanation of cadence, retention, or access.
[LP3] expected: Shell helper scripts are expected for launching and analyzing the screen workflow, but the skill does not provide a clear least-privilege tool scope.
[SDI-2] unexpected: The OS screenshot fallback captures the whole desktop when no portal frame is present; although listed in the manifest as a feature, it is not clearly surfaced in the runtime instructions as a separate sensitive mode.
[T05] unexpected: The unauthenticated network-accessible upload endpoint, wildcard CORS, and non-loopback service exposure are artifact-backed concerns for a screen-frame ingestion service.
[T09] unexpected: Unbounded request buffering and predictable shared temporary files are implementation weaknesses that increase denial-of-service, local disclosure, and frame-poisoning risk.
